title: Mendoza
description: A high desert at the foot of the Andes, irrigated by snowmelt, where Malbec found its second home.
L: Mendoza lies in western Argentina, at the foot of the Andes, near Aconcagua, the highest mountain outside Asia, at 6,961 m. It makes about 70% of Argentina's wine, with around 150,000 hectares of vines. Vineyards range from about 600 to 1,600 m in altitude.

Mendoza is a high desert, with about 200 to 250 mm of rain a year, in the Andes' rain shadow. Summers are hot and sunny, nights cool, with a large day and night swing. Low humidity means little disease. Hail is the biggest threat; many vineyards use hail nets. The Zonda, a hot, dry wind, can damage vines in spring.
What is the biggest weather threat in Mendoza?
Summer hailstorms can destroy crops; nets protect vines.

Without irrigation, Mendoza couldn't grow vines. Snowmelt from the Andes feeds rivers like the Mendoza and Tunuyán. The Huarpe people built channels before the Spanish arrived; the Spanish expanded them. Today, flood, furrow and drip irrigation all draw on this water. Water rights are precious, and drought years are a growing concern.
Mendoza's vineyards depend on irrigation from Andean snowmelt.
Yes. It's a desert without it.
Mendoza makes about 70% of Argentina's wine, under the Andes
It's a high, dry desert; hail is the main threat
Snowmelt irrigation, via ancient channels, makes it possible

Malbec is Mendoza's signature, with about 70% of Argentina's Malbec. It gives deep purple wines with plum, blackberry, violet and cocoa, and soft, ripe tannins. It arrived in 1853 with French agronomist Michel Aimé Pouget, hired to found an agricultural school. April 17, the date of the school's founding law, is now World Malbec Day.

Bonarda, the same as Douce Noir from Savoie, not Italy's Bonarda, is Argentina's second most planted red, giving fruity, soft wines. Cabernet Sauvignon is important, often blended with Malbec. Cabernet Franc has become a rising star. Whites include Chardonnay, Torrontés and Sémillon. Criolla Grande and Cereza, pink-skinned, make bulk wine.
Match each grape to its role.
Argentine Bonarda is not the same as Italian Bonarda. DNA shows it's Douce Noir, from France's Savoie.
Marking the 1853 founding of Mendoza's agricultural school.
Bonarda, Cabernet Sauvignon and Cabernet Franc follow

Luján de Cuyo lies just south of Mendoza city, at about 900 to 1,100 m, along the Mendoza river. It's Mendoza's historic quality heartland, sometimes called the first zone, primera zona, with Maipú. Sub-areas like Perdriel, Agrelo, Vistalba and Las Compuertas have deep alluvial soils with stones.

Luján de Cuyo has some of Argentina's oldest Malbec vines, many planted before 1950, on their own roots, since phylloxera spreads slowly in Mendoza's sandy, irrigated soils. In 1989, it became Argentina's first DOC, Denominación de Origen Controlada, for Malbec. Its wines are ripe, round and generous, with soft tannins.

Historic and famous producers include Catena Zapata, whose founder Nicolás Catena pioneered high-altitude, quality Malbec in the 1990s, Achával-Ferrer, Norton and Terrazas de los Andes. Many large wineries are based here, with vineyards both in Luján and in the Valle de Uco.
Which are sub-areas of Luján de Cuyo?
Gualtallary is in the Valle de Uco.
Luján de Cuyo is Mendoza's historic quality heart
It has old, own-rooted Malbec vines
It became Argentina's first DOC in 1989

The Valle de Uco lies about 100 km south-west of Mendoza city, at 900 to over 1,600 m, right against the Andes. Its three departments are Tupungato, Tunuyán and San Carlos. Since the 1990s, it's become Argentina's most acclaimed area for fine wine, with major investment, including from French and American producers.

Altitude cools the air by about 0.6 degrees per 100 m and strengthens ultraviolet light. Cool nights preserve acidity and aroma; strong UV thickens skins, adding colour and tannin. Valle de Uco Malbec is fresher, more floral and more structured than in Luján. Soils, alluvial with stones and limestone, vary greatly.
How does Valle de Uco Malbec usually compare with Luján de Cuyo's?

Since 2013, the Valle de Uco has recognised smaller GIs: Paraje Altamira, in San Carlos, with limestone-rich alluvial soils; Gualtallary, in Tupungato, high up to 1,600 m with limestone; Los Chacayes, in Tunuyán; and San Pablo, very high and cool. These help show terroir in Argentine wine.
Match each GI to its department.
The Valle de Uco has a growing map of GIs.
The Valle de Uco is high, against the Andes
Altitude gives fresher, more structured Malbec
GIs like Gualtallary and Paraje Altamira show terroir
Reading Mendoza and eating with it

Labels show the grape, often Malbec, the region, Mendoza, and increasingly a sub-region or GI, like Valle de Uco, Luján de Cuyo or Gualtallary. Altitude is often printed. Argentina requires 85% of a named grape. Reserva and Gran Reserva have minimum ageing rules for reds: 12 and 24 months.

Malbec is the wine of the asado, Argentina's barbecue: beef ribs, steak, chorizo and morcilla, blood sausage, with chimichurri, a herb and garlic sauce. Cabernet Franc suits lamb and herbs; Bonarda suits pizza and pasta; Torrontés suits empanadas. Serve Malbec at 16 to 18 degrees.
Which sauce is a classic with Malbec and steak?
Herbs, garlic and vinegar suit Malbec's fruit.
